title: Workday Pricing: Costs, Tiers and Discounts (2026)
summary: Workday pricing is entirely customized with no published rates. You'll know what cost factors to negotiate and what to budget for.
body_markdown:
## Connecting Workday to other systems with Activepieces


It won't lower what Workday quotes you, but[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/pricing) can shrink the integration line that tends to sit outside that quote.


It's a workflow automation tool with 744 integrations in an MIT-licensed core, and its pricing page lists what it costs before you add it to the comparison.


### Where integration cost appears in a Workday budget


Stop at the subscription and you've seen only the first invoice. Every hire that has to reach your payroll provider, your ticketing system or your chat tool is work someone gets paid to build and maintain.


That means a consulting statement of work, an internal admin's hours, or a middleware license, and none of them appear in the Workday quote.


If you price a retainer the way I do, you'd never hand a client a flat fee and then bill the glue work to a shared account.


Do the same here: put the glue on its own line, so one department's custom sync doesn't quietly ride on everyone else's budget.


### How per-run billing reduces workflow costs


Activepieces bills one credit per flow run, however many steps the flow has, so a ten-step sync costs the same as the two-step shortcut it replaced.


Zapier's per-task billing and Make's per-module billing, both on their own pricing pages, charge more as a flow is split into smaller parts, which taxes the builder for doing the job properly.


Here the run is the meter, not the steps inside it, and the glue line on your Workday budget doesn't grow when you make a flow more reliable. MoneyGram and Moneypenny run Activepieces in production, and the $20-a-month Plus plan includes 10,000 credits.


The run log on the left marks the step completed and the run as succeeded. The takeaway is how small the unit of work is: one event in one system, one message in another, with the mapping visible and testable.


Try the same shape on Workday-adjacent jobs. A new-hire event can create an account in another tool. An approval can post to the channel where approvers actually look.


Open any flow and you'll find a trigger, an action and a field mapping, which a non-developer can usually read and check.


The run history also gives you evidence of what fired and when, so you can see where the effort goes before you pay for more.


That's the scope: notifications, record handoffs and approvals between tools.


A run is 1 credit however many steps it has, and the Free plan gives you 1,000 credits a month with unlimited flows, so you can count your monthly runs against that allowance before paying anything.


### When not to use it


Skip it when the job is core to Workday itself: payroll logic, financial postings, or anything an auditor expects to trace inside the system of record.


Workday's own integration tooling, or a certified partner who already knows your tenant, is the better choice there, because accountability sits with one party.


Also skip it if nobody on your side will own the flows after launch. An unowned automation is a cost that moves from the invoice to an outage.
